hero.eyebrow: For students juggling more than one course
hero.title: Your studies, finally under control.
hero.subtitle: Connect your schedule, tell it what you are working towards, and get a study plan that fits the time you actually have — and adjusts when life changes.
hero.note: Free while in development. No card required.

problem.title: Planning shouldn't take longer than studying
problem.body: Three courses, two deadlines, a lecture schedule that shifts every week, and a vague sense of being behind. Most of the effort goes into working out what to do rather than doing it.

scattered.title: Everything lives somewhere else
scattered.body: Lectures in one calendar, deadlines in a course page, your own plans on paper.

unrealistic.title: Plans that were never possible
unrealistic.body: It is easy to write down thirty hours of work into a week that only has twelve free.

fragile.title: One missed session breaks everything
fragile.body: Miss a Tuesday and the whole plan needs rewriting by hand.

how.title: How it works
how.subtitle: Three steps, once. After that it maintains itself.

one.title: Bring your schedule
one.body: Import your university timetable, connect Google Calendar, or add courses by hand. Everything lands in one calendar.

two.title: Set your terms
two.body: When you focus best, how long a session should be, how much you can do in a day, and which courses matter most right now.

three.title: Get a plan you can keep
three.body: Study sessions placed around what you already have, with breaks protected and reasons given for every placement.

four.title: Keep it going
four.body: Join a study group with friends or coursemates and see how you are each doing at sticking to your own plan. Optional, and private to the group.

example.title: What a generated week looks like
example.subtitle: Study sessions placed around fixed commitments, with the reasoning shown.
example.explanation: Statistics has an exam in nine days, so it gets the two longest morning sessions when your energy is highest. Databases is spread across three shorter blocks because spaced revision holds better than one long push. Thursday is left lighter — you marked it as a low-energy day.
example.scrollLabel: Example week schedule. Scroll horizontally, or use the arrow keys, to see the full week.

groups.title: Studying alone is where plans quietly die
groups.subtitle: Add the people you already study with. You each keep your own plan and your own pace — the group just makes it harder to drift.
groups.note: Ranked on how much of your own plan you kept — never on hours, never on grades. A deliberately light week costs you nothing.

fair.title: A lighter week is not a loss
fair.body: Planning six hours and keeping all of them scores the same as planning thirty and keeping all of them.

private.title: Private and opt-in
private.body: Small invite-only groups. You choose what to share, and you can pause without leaving.

together.title: A shared goal, not just a ranking
together.body: The group has a target it reaches together, so a bad week for you is something the others can carry.

combined.title: One calendar for everything
combined.body: Several degree programs, imported timetables, personal events and study sessions in a single view.

realistic.title: It tells you when it doesn't fit
realistic.body: If you need thirty hours and have twelve, it says so — and offers concrete ways to close the gap.

adaptive.title: It recovers from a missed session
adaptive.body: Reschedule what you missed while changing as little of the rest of the week as possible.

explained.title: Every placement has a reason
explained.body: See why a session landed where it did, in plain language, and override it whenever you disagree.

recovery.title: Breaks are part of the plan
recovery.body: Lunch, rest and recovery are protected time, not whatever is left over.

portable.title: Take it with you
portable.body: Export to your calendar, a PDF, or an image. Your plan is not locked in here.

cta.title: Start with one week
cta.body: Add your courses, import a timetable, and see what a realistic week looks like. It takes about five minutes.

footer.notAffiliated: An independent project, not affiliated with any university.

audiences.title: Two kinds of week, one planner
audiences.subtitle: The scheduling is the same either way. What differs is where your time goes before you get to it — and what is worth measuring once you do.

student.title: Studying full time
student.body: Several courses, a timetable that shifts, and deadlines that arrive together. The hard part is not the work — it is knowing what to do on a Tuesday afternoon.

points.timetable: Import each programme's timetable; two degrees at once is normal here, and clashes are flagged rather than hidden.
points.exams: Exams and assignments set the pace, so the weeks before one fill up before the weeks after.
points.balance: Weekends stay yours unless you say otherwise.

student.metric: How much of your own plan you kept

professional.title: Studying alongside a job
professional.body: A certification, a language, a degree done in the evenings. The hard part is that the day is already spent by the time you get to it.

points.afterWork: Connect your work calendar and a full day at the office takes the evening with it — no study is planned on top of it.
points.realistic: Sessions are longer and later, and the weekly target starts at what survives a working week rather than what sounds ambitious.
points.protect: Meetings, applications and appointments go in the same list, so the plan bends around them instead of ignoring them.

professional.metric: Hours that survived the working week

intro.label: Get started
intro.todo: Read the brief and marking criteria, note every requirement and the deadline, gather what you need (data, sources, tools) and write down open questions.

work.label: Work on it
work.todo: Pick up where you left off and finish one concrete part — a section, an analysis, a draft.

finish.label: Finish & review
finish.todo: Check everything against the marking criteria, polish and proofread, then submit.

intro.label: Plan your revision
intro.todo: List the topics, find which lectures cover them, and mark the ones you know least.

work.label: Revise
work.todo: Work through your weakest topics, then test yourself with Quiz me on the Learn page.

finish.label: Practice run
finish.todo: Do a past paper or quiz yourself on everything, under time, and note what to look at once more.

howItWorks.title: How it works
howItWorks.description: What the planner does for you, the ways it can help you study, and what each study method means.

planning.title: How your week gets planned
planning.availability: You set when you can study (Settings → Study preferences). The planner only places sessions inside those hours and respects your daily limit.
planning.classes: Lectures, seminars, tutorials, labs and exams on your calendar always block study time — a study session never lands on top of a class.
planning.deadlines: Work is spread out before each deadline, with more time for bigger, harder and higher-priority tasks.
planning.startDate: Give a task a "Start studying from" date (e.g. exam revision late in the term) and nothing is scheduled for it before then.
planning.guided: Assignments and exams are planned as guided sessions: a short "Get started" session about two weeks before the deadline (read the brief, gather what you need), working sessions after it, and a final "Finish & review". Each session says what to do. Can't make one? Press "Can't do this", pick a day, and it moves there while the rest of the plan stays clear of it.
planning.logging: Press Start on a session to time it, and Finish to log the real minutes. Classes from the past week ask whether you attended; a missed one gets a Catch up button that summarises that lecture from its slides.
planning.studyStyle: Your study style (Settings) sets how long blocks are and how the timer behaves when you press Start: My own way (90-min blocks, no timer), Pomodoro 25/5 or 50/10 (2-hour blocks with focus and break rounds, with a notice and soft chime at each change), or Deep work (long blocks with a notice 10 minutes before the end). Back-to-back pieces of the same task are joined into one block. When you press Start you can also pick 52/17 (52 min focus, 17 min break) or a Sprint of any length. Tasks set to Active recall or Spaced repetition get a "Quiz me" button that opens a quiz on that course's material.
planning.replan: Plans are proposals: you review a plan before it is applied, and can regenerate it whenever things change.

learn.title: Studying with your course material
learn.intro: Each course has a "Study this course" page. Pick which lectures to use and how you want help:

modes.summary: A structured summary of the lectures you pick — the main ideas in order plus the key points to remember. Good for revision and for catching up on a missed lecture.
modes.explain: Name a topic and get it explained from the ground up, using your lecturer's own definitions and examples.
modes.ask: Ask a specific question and get a direct answer, with the slide or page it came from.
modes.quiz: Questions that test understanding, with the answers hidden until you are ready. Uses active recall — one of the most effective ways to remember.

learn.material: Answers only use the material you uploaded. If it doesn't cover something, you are told so rather than given a guess. Upload slides as PDF or PowerPoint (.pptx) on the course page.

methods.title: Study methods
methods.intro: You can give a task a preferred study method. It shapes how long its sessions are and how they are spread out.
methods.pomodoro: Short focused blocks (around 25 minutes) with short breaks. Good for getting started and for tasks that are hard to face.
methods.active_recall: Testing yourself instead of re-reading — close the notes and try to explain or answer. The quiz mode does this for you.
methods.spaced_repetition: Revisiting material in shorter sessions spread over days, so it sticks long-term. Best for exams.
methods.deep_work: Long uninterrupted blocks for demanding work like writing or problem sets.
methods.interleaving: Mixing different topics or problem types in one session, which builds the ability to tell them apart.
methods.group_work: Sessions meant for working with others, e.g. group projects or study groups.
